children.author: nine_k
children.text:
I assume the policy was written by rational, reasonable people, with a practical goal in mind: to prevent "AI slop", that is, dubious-quality, high-volume contributions by people who don't exactly understand how their PR works, and how the project works, but "computer says yes" because tests (which they also do not understand well) seem to pass.

If a submission (PR, bug report) is high-quality, and the person behind it is responsive and clueful, so that the useful parts of the submission can be taken, and problematic parts, fixed, then it does not matter what process has produced the code. It could as well be a Boltzmann brain [1].

Given that the author of the contribution actually got a grip on the problem, and on the solution, the limitation of "no AI use" is no longer load-bearing. Not only might it have been counterproductive — it's also unverifiable in practice. It becomes absurd, akin to a demand that the text must have been edited by Vim and not VSCode. It must be noted that a misguided policy may indeed force the contributor to delve in the depths of the process of PR creation, and showcase every manually undertaken step in an attempt to prove that no AI was involved. Ironically, it is no secret that many less scrupulous participants might leverage AI to imitate just that. It must be noted though that the decision ultimately belongs to the project maintainers.

(The above paragraph was hand-crafted for your and my entertainment.)

In short: by default I respect the authors of the policy and hence assume that they enact the policy for reasons that are rational, not religious.

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann_brain

>Again, use whatever tools, as long as your mind forms a clear understanding, which you can operate on independent on any LLMs or whatever.

that isn't what the policy says. It isn't just about writing the report.

> If you use a chatbot to give you advice on a comment on the issue tracker, that comment is unwelcome.

children.text:
They can't clarify it.

If you say the quiet part out loud, the lemmings will take that as approval.

"Only thoughtful application of AI allowed" -> "Of course my usage of AI was thoughtful! My custom pi harness with 1M context project brain is very thoughtful!"

Not sure why you think this wouldn't be something they did on principle either though. Most open source projects are built on someone's personal principles: that's what motivates them to keep working.

(hence the recommendation someone's free to fork it and do the work themselves)

The fact we have different interpretations is the reason why it should be clarified.

Some people reject AI on a matter of principle. They may have a problem with the energy cost, the idea that AI companies are stealing the world knowledge for their own profit, that any use of LLMs will make you stupid, or that it does more harm than good overall. The code of conduct links to a short story by Isaac Asimov, you typically don't do that when your motives are purely technical.

That's not my read, at least not if you give them enough credit to use their software.

My read is any LLM use should be opaque to them. You should be able to explain your bug find in your own words, have formatted as the project expects, not have any LLM generated comments (which trend towards being useless anyways)

The wording of the post is very clever, if you're green you read it and you say "I'm banned because I use Claude". If you're experienced enough you can read the message between the lines: "if you use LLMs, it should still have gone through your brain before it reaches mine, so I'm not turned into a meat puppet by proxy"

Then it should be clarified.

To me "no LLMs for finding bugs" means what it means, which implicitly means "we prefer to have bugs than for you to use a LLM". It is weird, may result in worse code, but it can be justified for ideological reasons, and I mean, why not, it is your project, your rules.

In the unlikely even I contribute one day, reading this rule, I will turn off my LLMs completely and my submissions will probably have bugs that could have been avoided using a LLM based debugging pass, but that's the rule, and I won't discuss it because it is also the rule.

If the intent is to avoid flooding maintainers with bug reports, say "no LLMs for bug reporting".

children.author: handoflixue
children.text:
> We know that if something gained somewhere, something lost somewhere.

Yeah, but that doesn't imply equivalent exchange.

If you care about being the best sprinter in the world, yeah, put in the time and effort! But if you just want to get to work, there's no way you can beat the speed of a car.

If you're one of the better bug-hunters in the world, you probably lose something by using an LLM. For the rest of us, it's increasingly like trying to race a car.

We definitely need both types - it's important having the humans who do have that top 1% understanding. But increasingly, for everyone else, LLMs outperform doing it by hand.

If an LLM finds a bug, is that almost the same as an LLM writing code for you? You can write lazy code as a sketch, for example without thinking about nested loops in your head, and then just use an LLM that will fix this loop in the bug report?
This can be viewed as a level of AI usage: 10% (for example), where vibe coding is 100%.
I think any percentage of usage affects your personal mental sharpness. We know that if something gained somewhere, something lost somewhere. The only question is where the "loss" is, and how it will affect everything and everyone.

"No LLMs for finding bugs." I really don't get rules such as these, plus they're not really enforceable. There's a difference between using the LLM to write the bug report and using the LLM to find the bug (if you suspect there is one) to then report after manual checking, in human words.

children.author: simoncion
children.text:
> ...is also completely unenforceable...

It's exactly as enforceable as when projects require you to swear that you can legally assign copyright of your submissions to the entity that runs the project, and/or swear that your submissions don't infringe on anyone's patents, and/or -as the ReactOS project does- swear that you've never seen the code that the project is reimplementing.

If someone swears that they're conforming to the rules and you later find out that they lied, then you ban them forever, publicly announce why, and -if needed- purge their contributions and do your best to alert affected users about the tainted versions. These sorts of policies work for the same reason ordinary doors and door locks work: most folks aren't profoundly antisocial shitbags.

> No LLMs for brainstorming and then sharing the results of that brainstorming, even if you create the prose.

I can understand the no automated AI contribution point of view, but going overboard with the above that is also completely unenforceable makes the policy look dumb.

children.text:
> I don't really care if someone can chain together zero-day exploits to "pwn" my lightbulbs.

The point of pwning your lightbulb is not to decide whether it's bright or dark in your house. It's valuable as a residential proxy with a good IP reputation, to be sold to the highest bidder who wants to do something they don't want traced to their own IP.

It really depends on what the application does. It's only really a problem if it's internet-facing, and even then, the harm is limited to the application's own permission set. I don't really care if someone can chain together zero-day exploits to "pwn" my lightbulbs.

A lot of the recent major exploits like php2shell require a fair amount of effort to use, so unless you're a major public figure or holding on to something very valuable, there's not a lot of reason to be concerned.

Obviously, if you're writing a password manager, it's a very different story and I'd be horrified by such a policy there. But you've got to make an argument that this specific app is actually a target

No LLMs for finding bugs.

As of late 2026, this is gross negligence and any project with such a policy should be assumed to have a variety of easily exploitable vulnerabilities.
